overview.intro:
Chapter 92 covers musical instruments and their parts: pianos and harpsichords (9201), guitars, violins, harps and other string instruments (9202), brass and woodwind instruments, accordions, harmonicas and pipe organs (9205), drums, cymbals and other percussion (9206), electric and electronic instruments such as electric guitars, digital pianos and synthesizers (9207), music boxes, whistles and decoy calls (9208), and parts, strings, stands and metronomes (9209). The U.S. imported **$1.39B** of these goods in 2025, 30% from China and 17% from Indonesia. **47 of 63** lines carry a base rate, from 2.6% (accordions) to **8.7%** (guitars over $100); cymbals, bagpipes, harmonicas, piano accordions, strings and most wind-instrument parts are Free.

On top of the base rate, the **2026 Section 301 duty** (from July 24, 2026) adds 10% or 12.5% for goods of 60 economies, with no product exemption in this chapter; for the EU and Taiwan it is a 10% floor and for Japan and South Korea a 12.5% floor in place of the lower base rate. **China** also pays the 7.5% List 4A duty on 58 lines (List 4B, which covers violins, other string instruments, music boxes and some stands, is suspended), so most Chinese instruments pay **20% to 28.7%**. **Brazil** adds 25%. Canadian and Mexican instruments that qualify for **USMCA** pay nothing; no Chapter 92 line is on the Section 338 lists for Canada, and no Section 232 or antidumping duty reaches the chapter. Instruments with **rosewood, ivory or tortoiseshell** also face Lacey Act and CITES rules: see Tariff engineering.

productGroups.label: Pianos: upright, grand & harpsichords
productGroups.blurb: Upright and grand pianos, player pianos, harpsichords and other keyboard stringed instruments: 12 lines at 4.7% (pianos) or 3.5% (other). Statistical lines split pianos by case height or length and separate used pianos. Japan, the biggest supplier, pays the 12.5% Section 301 floor; China pays 4.7% + 7.5% + 12.5% = 24.7%.

productGroups.label: Guitars, violins & other string instruments
productGroups.blurb: String instruments played with a bow (violins, violas, cellos, double basses, 3.2%) and other string instruments: acoustic guitars valued up to $100 without the case (4.5%) or over $100 (8.7%, the highest base rate in the chapter), and harps, mandolins, ukuleles and banjos (4.6%). Bowed instruments and 9202.90.60 are on China's suspended List 4B, so China pays only the 12.5% Section 301 duty on them.

productGroups.label: Brass, woodwind, accordions & pipe organs
productGroups.blurb: Wind instruments: brass (trumpets, trombones, horns, tubas; 2.9%), clarinets, saxophones and flutes (4.9%), harmoniums (2.7%), accordions (2.6%), and Free keyboard pipe organs, piano accordions, harmonicas (mouth organs), bagpipes and other wind instruments.

productGroups.label: Drums, cymbals & percussion
productGroups.blurb: Percussion instruments: drums (4.8%), cymbals (Free), chimes, peals and carillons (Free) and other percussion such as xylophones, tambourines, castanets and maracas (5.3%). Electronic drum kits are heading 9207.

productGroups.label: Electric guitars, digital pianos, keyboards & synths
productGroups.blurb: Instruments whose sound is produced or must be amplified electrically: keyboard instruments such as digital pianos, synthesizers and electronic organs (5.4%; 2.7% for Japan under the U.S.-Japan agreement, though Japan pays the 12.5% floor), and electric guitars, basses and other electric instruments (5%). The largest group: $552M in 2025.

productGroups.label: Music boxes, whistles & decoy calls
productGroups.blurb: Music boxes (3.2%) and other instruments not elsewhere covered: musical saws, mechanical organs, whistles, call horns and decoy calls of all kinds (5.3%). Music boxes are on China's suspended List 4B.

productGroups.label: Parts, strings, stands, metronomes & tuners
productGroups.blurb: Parts and accessories: instrument strings (Free), piano parts and tuning pins, guitar and violin parts, bows and chin rests (Free), mutes, drum pedals, music holders and collapsible stands (3.9% to 5.7%), parts for electric instruments (2.7%), and metronomes, tuning forks and pitch pipes (Free). Wind-instrument and music-box parts are Free.

workedExamples.title: $100,000 of electric guitars from China
workedExamples.body: Fretted electric string instruments have a **5%** base rate. China adds **7.5%** under Section 301 List 4A (9903.88.15) and **12.5%** under the 2026 Section 301 action (9903.05.31): **25%**, or **$25,000**. The List 4A exclusion for electric guitar kits has expired. Electric guitars of 9207.90.00.40 also need a Lacey Act plant declaration for their wood (phase VI, since October 1, 2021).

workedExamples.title: $50,000 of acoustic guitars from Indonesia, over $100 each
workedExamples.body: Guitars valued over $100 each, **excluding the value of the case**, have an **8.7%** base rate; at $100 or less they fall in 9202.90.20 at **4.5%**. Indonesia's 2026 Section 301 duty (9903.05.45) adds **10%**: **18.7%**, or **$9,350**. Declare the unit value without the case, since a case entered with the guitar is classified with it but does not count toward the $100 break.

workedExamples.title: A grand piano from Japan
workedExamples.body: Grand pianos have a **4.7%** general rate and are Free under the U.S.-Japan Trade Agreement (SPI JP). Since July 24, 2026 Japanese goods with a column 1 rate under 12.5% pay a flat **12.5%** in place of it (9903.05.49), so a $60,000 grand piano pays **$7,500** whether or not the agreement is claimed. Before July 2026 the same piano paid the 15% all-in reciprocal rate (until February 24, 2026) and then the 10% Section 122 surcharge (until July 23, 2026).

workedExamples.title: Digital pianos and keyboards from China vs Malaysia vs Mexico
workedExamples.body: Keyboard instruments of 9207.10 have a **5.4%** base rate. From **China** they pay 5.4% + 7.5% (List 4A) + 12.5% = **25.4%**; from **Malaysia** 5.4% + 10% (9903.05.54) = **15.4%**; from **Mexico** they are **Free** with a USMCA certification of origin and 15.4% without (5.4% + 10%, 9903.05.55).

workedExamples.title: A violin from China
workedExamples.body: Bowed string instruments have a **3.2%** base rate. 9202.10 is on Section 301 List 4B (9903.88.16), which is suspended (U.S. note 20(t)–(u)), so a Chinese violin pays only 3.2% + **12.5%** (9903.05.31) = **15.7%**. A bow entered with the violin in normal numbers is classified with it (Chapter 92 note 2). A violin with an ivory fitting or a pernambuco bow needs CITES and FWS clearance as well.

tariffUpdates.h1: HTS Chapter 92: Musical Instruments Tariff Rates — Tariff Updates

seo.title: Musical Instrument Tariff Updates 2025–2026: China, Section 301, IEEPA, USMCA (HTS Ch. 92) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: What changed for U.S. imports of pianos, guitars, drums, wind instruments and keyboards since January 2025: the IEEPA duties and their end, the Section 122 surcharge, the 2026 Section 301 duties on 60 economies, Brazil, China List 4A, and the CITES and Lacey Act changes, with official citations.

tariffUpdates.intro:
This page compares two editions of the tariff schedule: the **2025 Basic Edition**, in force at the start of 2025, and the current **2026 Revision 21** (in force October 9, 2026). The base rates of all 63 Chapter 92 lines are unchanged.

The extra duties changed a lot. In 2025 musical instruments paid every IEEPA duty in full, since no Chapter 92 line was on an exemption annex: 25% on non-USMCA goods of Canada (35% from August 1) and Mexico, 10% to 20% fentanyl duties and a reciprocal duty on China, the reciprocal tariff on everyone else (country rates from August 7, 2025, for example 19% for Indonesia and Malaysia, 20% for Vietnam and 15% all-in for the EU and Japan), and 40% on Brazil. All IEEPA duties **ended on February 24, 2026**; the 10% **Section 122** surcharge that replaced them expired on **July 23, 2026**.

Today three measures apply: the **2026 Section 301 duties** on 60 economies (from July 24, 2026, no product exemption in this chapter), **Brazil's 25% Section 301 duty** (from July 22, 2026), and China's Section 301 **List 4A** duty of 7.5% on 58 lines, which USTR continued on October 7, 2026. No Section 232, Section 338 or antidumping/countervailing duty reaches Chapter 92. Wildlife and plant rules changed too: CITES exempted finished instruments of rosewood from November 26, 2019, and amended the pernambuco (bow wood) listing from March 5, 2026.
tariffUpdates.scope: Chapter 99 measures that reach Chapter 92 from any country (2026 Section 301 on 60 economies, Brazil Section 301, China Section 301 List 4A; the ended IEEPA and Section 122 duties; the Section 338 lists on Canada, which name no Chapter 92 line), plus the FWS (CITES, ivory) and APHIS (Lacey Act) changes that affect instrument imports. No antidumping or countervailing duty order covers Chapter 92 goods. For the rate each supplier pays, see Rates by country.

inEffect.exemption: The 7.5% List 4A duty (9903.88.15, U.S. note 20(r)–(s)) covers 58 of 63 lines; the other 5 (9202.10, 9202.90.60, 9208.10, 9209.92.20, 9209.94.40) are on List 4B (9903.88.16), which is suspended. The List 4A product exclusions for acoustic pianos, acoustic guitars valued up to $100, harp sharping levers, electric guitar kits and synthesizer circuit boards (U.S. note 20) have all expired. No Chapter 92 line is on List 3. Note 52(a) keeps the List 4A duty on top of the 12.5%. No Chapter 92 line is on the general exemption list in U.S. note 52(b) or on any note 52(j) country list, so the duty reaches all 63 lines. The IEEPA duties on China ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Chapter 92 base rates: no changes
changes.detail: All 63 Chapter 92 tariff lines carry the same General, Special and Column 2 rates in the 2026 Revision 21 as in the 2025 Basic Edition.

changes.title: China Section 301 actions continue during the four-year review
changes.detail: USTR announced that the Section 301 actions on China, including the 7.5% List 4A duty on 58 Chapter 92 lines, continue while the review proceeds. No Chapter 92 product exclusion is in effect.

changes.title: Section 338 on Canada: no Chapter 92 lines
changes.detail: Proclamations 11046 to 11048 imposed a 50% duty on products of Canada on the lists in U.S. note 51(b), applied from August 22, 2026 (Proclamation 11056) and changed from September 15, 2026 (Proclamations 11064 and 11065). None of the lists names a Chapter 92 line, so Canadian instruments stay Free with a USMCA claim.

changes.title: 2026 Section 301 duties on 60 economies
changes.detail: The 10% or 12.5% Section 301 duties on 60 economies (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) took effect and reach all 63 Chapter 92 lines: no instrument is on the general exemption list (U.S. note 52(b)) or a note 52(j) country list. For the EU and Taiwan the duty is a 10% floor and for Japan, South Korea and Switzerland a 12.5% floor in place of the lower base rate. Canadian and Mexican goods entered under USMCA are exempt (notes 52(g)–(h)), and the China List 4A duty stays on top (note 52(a)).

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge expired
changes.detail: The 150-day 10% surcharge (9903.03.01) expired at the close of July 23, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil Section 301: 25% on all Chapter 92 goods
changes.detail: The 25% Section 301 duty on goods of Brazil (9903.05.01) took effect. No Chapter 92 line is on its exemption list (U.S. note 50(a)(ii)), so it reaches all 63 lines and stacks with the 12.5% 2026 Section 301 duty from July 24.

changes.title: USMCA joint review: not renewed, still in force
changes.detail: The United States did not agree to renew the USMCA in its current form. USTR said the Agreement remains in force pending resolution of the issues or until termination, so USMCA claims (SPI S) still make Canadian and Mexican instruments Free.

changes.title: De minimis suspension made indefinite
changes.detail: The $800 duty-free de minimis exemption has been suspended for all countries since August 29, 2025 (Executive Order 14324), kept after the IEEPA ruling (Executive Order 14388), and suspended indefinitely for all modes other than the postal network by CBP's interim final rule of June 24, 2026. Low-value parcels of strings, picks and other parts need an entry and pay the full duty.

changes.title: CITES: pernambuco (bow wood) listing amended
changes.detail: The CoP20 amendments took effect. Annotation #10 for pernambuco (Paubrasilia echinata), the wood of most fine violin bows, now covers all parts and derivatives except finished instruments, parts and accessories moved non-commercially (performance, personal use, repair and similar) without a change of ownership, with a zero quota for wild-harvested specimens traded commercially. Commercial imports of new pernambuco bows need a pre-Convention certificate or a CITES permit for a non-wild source.

changes.title: Section 122 surcharge replaces the IEEPA tariffs
changes.detail: A 10% surcharge on products of all countries (9903.03.01) applied until July 23, 2026, to every Chapter 92 line. Canadian and Mexican goods entered under USMCA were exempt (9903.03.07, 9903.03.08).

changes.title: All IEEPA tariffs end
changes.detail: After the Supreme Court held on February 20, 2026 (Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump) that IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, Executive Order 14389 ended the Canada, Mexico, China, Brazil and reciprocal duties, and CBP stopped collecting them for goods entered from 12:01 a.m. ET on February 24, 2026.

changes.title: AGOA reauthorized
changes.detail: AGOA was reauthorized through December 31, 2026, retroactive to September 30, 2025. Every dutiable Chapter 92 line is Free under AGOA (SPI D) for eligible sub-Saharan African countries; GSP (SPI A) stays expired.

changes.title: Section 301 tariff on Nicaragua phases in from 2027
changes.detail: Products of Nicaragua that are not CAFTA-DR originating goods will pay +10% from January 1, 2027 and +15% from January 1, 2028 (9903.89.01, U.S. note 29), on every Chapter 92 line. The rate is 0% in 2026.

changes.title: Japan: 15% all-in reciprocal rate
changes.detail: Executive Order 14345 set the reciprocal duty on Japanese goods to 15% including the base rate, retroactive to goods entered from August 7, 2025,, so Japanese pianos, wind instruments and keyboards paid 15% in all until February 24, 2026.

changes.title: De minimis exemption suspended for all countries
changes.detail: Executive Order 14324 ended duty-free entry for shipments valued at $800 or less from every country, effective for goods entered from August 29, 2025.

changes.title: Country-specific reciprocal rates take effect
changes.detail: Executive Order 14326 replaced the 10% baseline with country-specific reciprocal rates for many partners, for example 19% for Indonesia and Malaysia, 20% for Vietnam, 15% all-in for the EU and Japan, and 10% for the United Kingdom. Every Chapter 92 line paid them. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Brazil: 40% IEEPA duty
changes.detail: Executive Order 14323 added a 40% duty on products of Brazil (9903.01.77) on top of the 10% reciprocal duty. No Chapter 92 line was on its Annex I exceptions (U.S. note 2(x)(iii)). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Canada additional duty raised to 35%
changes.detail: Raised the IEEPA duty on non-USMCA Canadian goods from 25% to 35% (9903.01.10). Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: China IEEPA duties: reciprocal rate cut to 10%
changes.detail: Chinese instruments paid IEEPA duties on top of Section 301: a fentanyl-related 10% from February 4, 2025 (20% from March 4, back to 10% from November 10, 2025) and a reciprocal duty that rose to 125% in April 2025 and was cut to 10% from May 14, 2025. A Chinese electric guitar paid 5% + 7.5% + 20% + 10% = 42.5% in mid-2025. All ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Reciprocal tariff: 10% baseline on all Chapter 92 goods
changes.detail: 10% baseline (9903.01.25) on products of all countries except Canada and Mexico from April 5, 2025. No Chapter 92 line was on Annex II (U.S. note 2(v)(iii)), so every instrument paid it. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: USMCA goods exempted from the Canada and Mexico duties
changes.detail: From March 7, 2025, goods entered under USMCA were exempt from the IEEPA duties on Canada and Mexico. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Additional duties on products of Canada and Mexico
changes.detail: +25% on goods of Canada (9903.01.10) and Mexico (9903.01.01), in force from March 4, 2025. Ended February 24, 2026.

changes.title: Lacey Act declaration extended to drums, woodwinds and electric guitars
changes.detail: APHIS began enforcing the plant import declaration for bagpipes, clarinets, flutes and other woodwinds (9205.90.20, 9205.90.40), drums (9206.00.20), fretted electric string instruments (9207.90.00.40), parts of string instruments (9209.92) and of bagpipes and woodwinds, and other parts (9209.99.80). understandIndustry.why:
U.S. imports of Chapter 92 goods were **$1.39B in 2025**, down 15.2% from $1.64B in 2024 and well below the 2022 peak of $1.98B. **China** supplied $421M (30%), down 28.5% in a year of IEEPA duties that reached 42.5% on a Chinese electric guitar: mostly electric instruments and keyboards ($172M), acoustic guitars ($71M), wind instruments ($67M) and parts ($63M). **Indonesia** ($233M, 17%) ships mostly digital pianos, keyboards and electric instruments ($162M) plus acoustic guitars and pianos; **Japan** ($135M) pianos ($46M) and wind instruments ($45M); **Mexico** ($119M, the only large supplier that grew) electric instruments ($54M) and guitars ($53M), mostly Free under USMCA. Taiwan, reported by Comtrade as "Other Asia, nes" ($84M), ships wind instruments, drums and parts; **Malaysia** ($60M) electric instruments; **Germany** ($59M) parts, pianos and wind instruments.

By product, electric instruments lead: 9207.90 (electric guitars and basses) was $349M and 9207.10 (digital pianos and synthesizers) $203M, together 40% of the chapter. Brass instruments (9205.10, down 30.9%), other wind instruments (9205.90, down 27.9%) and grand pianos (9201.20, down 25.2%) fell the most; strings (9209.30, up 20.8%) and upright pianos rose.

2025 is the latest full year of U.S. trade data, so the figures show the IEEPA duties but not the 2026 Section 301 and Brazil duties. Duty-collected figures aren't available from an official source yet.

tariffEngineering.h1: HTS Chapter 92: Musical Instruments — Import Documents & Ways to Lower Duty

seo.title: Importing Musical Instruments: CITES Rosewood, Ivory, Lacey Act and Legal Ways to Lower Duty (HTS Ch. 92) | KoalaGains
seo.shortDescription: Tariff engineering for HTS Chapter 92: the $100 guitar value break, classification of kits, sets, amplifiers and pedals, USMCA, first-sale valuation, drawback and Chapter 98, plus the Lacey Act declaration, CITES rosewood and pernambuco rules, ivory and tortoiseshell bans and FWS clearance.

tariffEngineering.intro:
The duty on an instrument depends on three facts: **what it is** (an acoustic guitar over or under $100 without its case, an electric guitar, a digital piano, a part, or an amplifier or pedal that belongs in Chapter 85), **where it was made** (China pays up to 28.7%, Mexico and Canada nothing with USMCA, Japan and the EU a flat floor) and **its value** (first sale, assists, the case). Those are the levers below.

Instruments are also wildlife and plant products. Wooden instruments need a **Lacey Act** plant declaration naming each species; rosewood, ebony and other listed woods, pernambuco bows, **elephant ivory** keys and fittings, **tortoiseshell**, bone, mother-of-pearl and reptile skins bring in **CITES** and **FWS** rules, including bans on commercial imports of ivory and tortoiseshell. Each rule and lever links to its regulation.

levers.title: Classify by type and value: acoustic vs electric, the $100 guitar break, instrument vs accessory
levers.saves: Up to 4.2 points on guitars (8.7% over $100 vs 4.5% at or under $100, both excluding the case); amplifiers (8518.40.20, Free) and effects pedals (8543.70.98.20, 2.6%) are not Chapter 92 goods
levers.appliesTo: Guitars (9202.90.20 / .40), electric instruments (9207), parts and accessories (9209), and accessories classified outside the chapter
levers.document: The unit value without the case on the invoice, a product description (acoustic, electric, keyboard), and for kits and sets the list of components. Unassembled instruments and complete kits are classified as the finished instrument (General Rule of Interpretation 2(a)); bows and sticks entered with their instrument go with it (Chapter 92 note 2). A binding ruling under 19 CFR part 177 settles a close case before import.
levers.caveat: Classification follows what the goods are; splitting the case from the guitar or undervaluing to land under $100 is not allowed. Amplifiers, microphones and other Chapter 85 accessories stay outside Chapter 92 only when not built into the instrument (note 1(b)).

levers.title: Claim USMCA for Mexican and Canadian instruments
levers.saves: The base rate (up to 8.7%) plus the 10% 2026 Section 301 duty on Mexico (9903.05.55) or Canada (9903.05.29)
levers.appliesTo: Originating goods of Mexico and Canada, such as Mexican guitars and electric instruments
levers.document: A USMCA certification of origin from the importer, exporter or producer, in the importer's possession when the claim is made (19 CFR 182.12). Rules of origin: General Note 11.
levers.caveat: Instruments assembled in Mexico from Asian parts must meet the product-specific rule. The USMCA was not renewed at the July 1, 2026 joint review but remains in force.

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. note 52(g)–(h)
USTR statement on the USMCA joint review (July 1, 2026)

levers.title: Know the country of origin and the rate it carries
levers.saves: The gap between origins: 25% on a Chinese electric guitar vs 15% from Indonesia or Malaysia, 10% flat from the EU or Taiwan, Free from Mexico with USMCA
levers.document: Production records showing where the instrument was substantially transformed (made into a new article with a new name, character and use), and the matching origin marking.
levers.caveat: Final assembly or finishing of a Chinese instrument elsewhere may not change its origin; CBP decides by substantial transformation, and a ruling can confirm it. Mis-declaring origin is fraud.

levers.title: Value at the first sale for export when you buy through a middleman
levers.saves: Duty on the middleman's markup: on a $300 guitar bought for $240 at the factory, 25% duty on $60 less ($15 per guitar from China)
levers.appliesTo: Instruments bought through a trading company or brand owner that bought them from the factory
levers.document: The factory-to-middleman invoice and proof the sale was at arm's length and the goods were clearly destined for the United States (19 U.S.C. 1401a; 19 CFR 152.103).
levers.caveat: Assists (molds, designs, parts supplied free) and royalties must be added to the value (19 CFR 152.103); CBP can ask for the full transaction chain.

levers.title: Use Chapter 98 for repairs abroad, American goods returned and instruments on tour
levers.saves: Duty only on the repair cost abroad (9802.00.40/.50), no duty on U.S.-made instruments returned unchanged (9801.00.10), and no duty on instruments brought in temporarily under bond or ATA Carnet (9813.00)
levers.appliesTo: Instruments sent abroad for repair, U.S.-made instruments coming back, and professional instruments for performances
levers.document: Export and repair records (19 CFR 10.8), proof of U.S. origin (19 CFR 10.1), or a temporary-importation bond or ATA Carnet (19 CFR 10.31); instruments with ivory, rosewood or other listed parts also need their CITES or musical instrument certificate.
levers.caveat: A repair that makes a new or different article does not qualify, and a TIB must be exported within the bond period.

levers.title: Claim drawback when the instruments, or goods made from them, are exported
levers.saves: Generally 99% of the duties paid, including the Section 301 duties and the base rate, on goods re-exported unused or used to make exported goods
levers.document: A drawback claim to CBP with the import and export records (19 CFR part 191); the claim is generally 99% of the eligible duties (19 CFR 191.51).
levers.caveat: Claims must be filed within five years of import, and the export or destruction must be documented.

rules.title: Lacey Act: instruments of illegally taken wood may not be imported (16 U.S.C. 3372(a)); a plant import declaration with the scientific name, value, quantity and country of harvest of each wood is required (7 CFR 357.3). APHIS enforces it for pianos and string instruments (9201, 9202) since April 1, 2010, and for woodwinds, bagpipes, drums, fretted electric instruments and string- and woodwind-instrument parts since October 1, 2021; goods with no plant content, or where plant material is no more than 5% of the weight (and not a CITES or endangered species), are excepted (7 CFR 357.4)

rules.agency: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service / APHIS / CBP
rules.title: CITES timber: finished instruments, finished parts and finished accessories of Dalbergia rosewoods and bubinga are exempt under annotation #15 (since November 26, 2019); unfinished rosewood parts, fingerboard blanks and other listed woods need CITES export documents, and Brazilian rosewood (Dalbergia nigra, Appendix I since June 11, 1992) needs a pre-Convention certificate. Plant shipments clear through designated ports

citations.label: FWS notice: CoP18 changes to CITES listings (September 9, 2019)
FWS: wood, timber and other tree products

rules.title: Pernambuco (Paubrasilia echinata) bows: since March 5, 2026 annotation #10 covers all parts and derivatives except finished instruments, parts and accessories moved non-commercially without a change of ownership; wild-harvested pernambuco has a zero commercial quota, so a commercial import of a new bow needs a pre-Convention certificate (wood from before September 13, 2007) or a CITES permit for a non-wild source

African elephant ivory (piano keys, bow frogs and tips, bagpipe mounts): commercial import of worked ivory is prohibited; an instrument with ivory acquired before February 26, 1976 may cross the border non-commercially with a CITES musical instrument certificate and must not be sold abroad (50 CFR 17.40(e)(5)(i)). Asian elephant ivory and hawksbill tortoiseshell are endangered species and Appendix I

Instruments and parts containing wildlife (ivory, bone, tortoiseshell, mother-of-pearl, snake or lizard skin, horsehair is domesticated and exempt) must be declared to FWS on Form 3-177, enter at a designated port and be cleared before CBP releases them; commercial importers need an FWS import/export license

Other CITES wildlife parts (for example python or lizard skin on drums and banjos, some shells) need the CITES export permit or re-export certificate for their appendix, and an import permit for Appendix I species

Electronic instruments with digital circuitry (digital pianos, synthesizers, electronic drums) are generally Part 15 digital devices: they must meet the FCC equipment authorization rules before they are imported or marketed

Instruments designed or intended primarily for children 12 or younger are children's products (lead and testing rules, Children's Product Certificate); a general-use instrument stays general-use even when sold to schools. Toy instruments are heading 9503, not Chapter 92
Country-of-origin marking: each instrument, or its retail container when the article cannot be marked, must show the origin legibly and permanently enough to reach the ultimate purchaser

Report the Chapter 99 numbers with the Chapter 92 line: the 2026 Section 301 heading for the country (9903.05.20–9903.05.84) or the USMCA exemption (9903.05.93/.94), China List 4A (9903.88.15), Brazil (9903.05.01)

citations.label: HTSUS Ch. 99, subch. III, U.S. notes 20, 50 and 52

rules.title: USMCA claims: a certification of origin in the importer's possession, provided to CBP on request

groups.label: Pianos: upright, grand & harpsichords
groups.note: Pianos need a Lacey Act declaration for their wood (since 2010). Old pianos with ivory keys may not be imported commercially; Brazilian rosewood cases need a pre-Convention certificate. Antique pianos over 100 years old are heading 9706, Free.

groups.label: Guitars, violins & other string instruments
groups.note: Guitars, violins and other string instruments need a Lacey Act declaration. Finished rosewood instruments are CITES-exempt; Brazilian rosewood is Appendix I; commercial imports of pernambuco bows need CITES documents; ivory fittings are restricted.

groups.label: Brass, woodwind, accordions & pipe organs
groups.note: Woodwinds and bagpipes need a Lacey Act declaration (since 2021); African blackwood (Dalbergia melanoxylon) clarinets are finished instruments exempt under annotation #15. Bagpipes with ivory mounts need FWS clearance; harmoniums, accordions and harmonicas are in the proposed phase VII.

groups.label: Drums, cymbals & percussion
groups.note: Drums need a Lacey Act declaration (since 2021); drums with wildlife skins need FWS clearance and CITES documents for listed species.

groups.label: Electric guitars, digital pianos, keyboards & synths
groups.note: Fretted electric instruments need a Lacey Act declaration (since 2021); digital keyboards and synthesizers fall under FCC digital-device rules. Amplifiers and effects pedals are Chapter 85.

groups.label: Music boxes, whistles & decoy calls
groups.note: Music boxes, whistles and decoy calls: origin marking; toy versions are heading 9503.

groups.label: Parts, strings, stands, metronomes & tuners
groups.note: Parts of string and woodwind instruments need a Lacey Act declaration (since 2021). Finished rosewood fingerboards and bridges ready to install are CITES-exempt finished parts; blanks are not. Strings and parts carry no extra wildlife rules unless they contain listed species.

tariffEngineering.disclaimer: A checklist of where the rules are, with links to the regulations; not legal advice. CITES listings change at each Conference of the Parties; check the species of every wood and animal part with FWS before importing.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on musical instruments?
searchedAs: are there tariffs on musical instruments
are musical instruments exempt from tariffs
faqs.answer: Yes. Every Chapter 92 line has a base rate of Free to 8.7%, and since July 24, 2026 goods of 60 economies pay the 2026 Section 301 duty on top: +10% or +12.5%, or a flat 10% (EU, Taiwan) or 12.5% (Japan, South Korea, Switzerland) in place of the base rate. No instrument is exempt from it. China also pays 7.5% on most lines and Brazil 25%. Mexican and Canadian instruments that qualify for USMCA are Free. The IEEPA tariffs ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on musical instruments and guitars from China?
searchedAs: tariffs on musical instruments from china
faqs.answer: Most Chinese instruments pay the base rate plus 7.5% (Section 301 List 4A, 9903.88.15) plus 12.5% (2026 Section 301, 9903.05.31): 24.7% on pianos, 25% on electric guitars, 25.4% on digital pianos and keyboards, 24.5% on acoustic guitars up to $100 and 28.7% over $100. Violins and other bowed instruments, 9202.90.60 string instruments, music boxes and two kinds of stands are on the suspended List 4B and pay base + 12.5% (15.7% on a violin).

faqs.question: What is the tariff on musical instruments from Japan?
searchedAs: tariffs on musical instruments from japan
tariff on musical instruments from japan
faqs.answer: A flat 12.5% on every Chapter 92 line (9903.05.49), because Japanese goods with a column 1 rate under 12.5% pay 12.5% in place of it. That covers pianos, brass and woodwind instruments, guitars, keyboards and parts, including lines that are Free under the U.S.-Japan Trade Agreement. Japan supplied $135M in 2025, mostly pianos and wind instruments.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on musical instruments from Germany and the EU?
searchedAs: tariffs on musical instruments from germany
european union tariffs on acoustic guitars
tariff on musical instruments from germany
faqs.answer: A flat 10% on every Chapter 92 line (9903.05.39): EU goods with a column 1 rate under 10% pay 10% in place of it, and every Chapter 92 rate is below 10%. That applies to German pianos and parts, Italian accordions, French woodwinds and Austrian brass alike. The 15% IEEPA rate ended February 24, 2026.

faqs.question: Are there tariffs on musical instruments from Canada and Mexico?
faqs.answer: Not on instruments that qualify for USMCA: they are Free, and exempt from the 2026 Section 301 duty (notes 52(g)–(h)). No Chapter 92 line is on Canada's Section 338 lists. Without a USMCA claim they pay the base rate plus 10%, for example 18.7% on a guitar over $100. This answers the U.S. tariff on imports; Canada's tariffs on U.S. guitars are set by Canada.

faqs.question: What is the tariff on brass and band instruments?
searchedAs: tariffs on brass instruments in usa
faqs.answer: Brass instruments (9205.10: trumpets, trombones, horns, tubas) have a 2.9% base rate, and clarinets, saxophones and flutes (9205.90.40) 4.9%. From China they pay 22.9% and 24.9%, from Taiwan or the EU 10%, from Japan 12.5%, from India 12.9% and 14.9%. Bagpipes and harmonicas are Free at base.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a guitar?
faqs.answer: Acoustic guitars are 9202.90: 9202.90.20 if valued not over $100 each excluding the case (4.5%), 9202.90.40 if over $100 (8.7%). Electric guitars and basses are 9207.90 (5%; 9207.90.00.40 for fretted string instruments). Unassembled guitars and complete kits are classified as guitars. Used guitars use the same codes; antiques over 100 years old are 9706 (Free).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for guitar strings, parts, pedals and cases?
faqs.answer: Strings are 9209.30 (Free). Parts of acoustic guitars are 9209.92.80 (4.6%) and of electric guitars 9209.94.80 (2.7%); collapsible stands 9209.92.20 or 9209.94.40. Outside Chapter 92: effects pedals 8543.70.98.20 (2.6%), amplifiers 8518.40.20 (Free), clip-on tuners 9031.80.80.85, and instrument cases 4202.92.50 (4.2%) when entered separately.

faqs.question: What is the HS code for a piano or digital piano?
faqs.answer: Acoustic upright pianos are 9201.10 and grand pianos 9201.20 (both 4.7%), with statistical suffixes by case height or length and for used pianos; harpsichords are 9201.90 (3.5%). Digital pianos, keyboards and synthesizers are 9207.10 (5.4%). Piano parts are 9209.91 (tuning pins Free, other parts 4.2%).

faqs.question: What is the HS code for drums and a drum set?
searchedAs: hs code for percussion musical instruments
faqs.answer: Acoustic drums and drum sets are 9206.00.20 (4.8%), cymbals 9206.00.40 (Free) and other percussion 9206.00.80 (5.3%). Electronic drum kits are 9207.90. Drumsticks entered with drums in normal numbers are classified with them (Chapter 92 note 2); drum pedals and holders for cymbals are 9209.99.10 (5.7%).

faqs.question: Do I need a CITES permit for a rosewood guitar?
faqs.answer: Not for a finished guitar of Indian, East Indian or other Dalbergia rosewood or bubinga: since November 26, 2019 CITES annotation #15 exempts finished musical instruments, finished parts and finished accessories. Unfinished rosewood parts and blanks still need CITES documents. Brazilian rosewood (Dalbergia nigra) is Appendix I: a guitar made with it needs a pre-Convention certificate showing the wood predates June 11, 1992. A Lacey Act declaration is still required.

faqs.question: What is a CITES musical instrument certificate (passport)?
faqs.answer: A passport-like CITES document (FWS Form 3-200-88) for traveling musicians whose instrument contains protected species, such as ivory, Brazilian rosewood or tortoiseshell. It is valid up to three years for multiple non-commercial border crossings, the holder must live in the United States, and the instrument may not be sold while abroad. Finished pernambuco bows moved non-commercially need no document since March 5, 2026.

faqs.question: Can I import a piano with ivory keys?
faqs.answer: Not for sale: commercial import of African elephant worked ivory is prohibited (50 CFR 17.40(e)). An instrument with ivory acquired before February 26, 1976 may be imported non-commercially, for example a musician's own piano or violin, with a CITES musical instrument certificate, if it is marked to match the certificate and not sold abroad. It must be declared to FWS and enter through a designated port.

faqs.question: What does the Lacey Act require for guitars and other instruments?
faqs.answer: The Lacey Act bans importing instruments made of wood taken or traded in violation of law, and APHIS requires a plant import declaration naming each wood species, the value, quantity and country of harvest. It is enforced for pianos and acoustic string instruments since 2010 and for woodwinds, drums, electric guitars and string-instrument parts since October 1, 2021. Products with no plant content, or 5% or less plant material by weight (not CITES species), are excepted.

faqs.question: Where does the U.S. import musical instruments from?
faqs.answer: Mostly Asia: China $421M (30% of the $1.39B imported in 2025), Indonesia $233M, Japan $135M, Mexico $119M, Taiwan $84M, Malaysia $60M, Germany $59M, Canada $43M and South Korea $39M. Electric guitars and basses (9207.90, $349M) and digital pianos and synthesizers (9207.10, $203M) are the biggest products. Imports fell 15.2% from 2024.
